24bc3df559.q: How did early experience in PVC window manufacturing during the 1980s shape understanding of fenestration production?
24bc3df559.a: John started at a small fabricator in Lancashire in the mid-1980s making PVC windows during the early days of PVC. He spent his first 18 months on manufacturing, progressing through order processing, purchasing, and laying out bays, learning manufacturing from start to finish through trial and error with no technical manuals or support from system houses.

88f67651bc.q: What is the biggest change in the fenestration industry over the past 40 years?
88f67651bc.a: The biggest change has been driven by standards and regulations pushing product quality much higher. Products from the 1980s were basic and insecure, but today all systems meet requirements of PAS24 and Secure by Design when assembled correctly, and consumers get far better products in terms of both security and energy performance.

f09c96ee34.q: What is the typical failure rate for windows and doors during certification testing?
f09c96ee34.a: John states that the chances of products getting through everything without a single issue is pretty unlikely. The failure rate is around 70% per visit when clients come with a range of windows and doors for testing for weather, security, and other factors, though failures can be due to fabrication issues, component issues, or other reasons.

dd7826b97a.q: Why are trickle vents problematic in modern thermally efficient windows?
dd7826b97a.a: Trickle vents destroy the thermal performance of highly efficient windows by putting holes through them. A government study published in 2019 found that trickle vents don't work effectively because when they are needed most—at night with curtains closed—there is no airflow, and they only work if wind is blowing, which would cause occupants to close them anyway.

e851c30e44.q: What is the PLC scheme and how does it differ from other thermal performance certification databases?
e851c30e44.a: The PLC scheme, which stands for Part L Compliance, was set up last year and provides approvals for energy ratings and U-values for windows and doors. Unlike other schemes that only show a company can make an A-rated window without detail, PLC details the frame, glass type, and approval specifications on the website, making it transparent and searchable with filters to find exactly what specification is needed.

88a24cafdc.q: How many product approvals are currently registered on the PLC scheme database?
88a24cafdc.a: ER Certification has several companies on the PLC scheme now, up to about 80 approval companies, with one company in particular holding over two and a half thousand approvals on the database, which customers can filter and drill down to find exactly what they need.

850b960673.q: Why does ER Certification not engage in fire door certification despite industry demand?
850b960673.a: Testing and certifying fire doors is a very expensive and costly undertaking. While ER Certification does certify companies manufacturing fire-rated units through cascaded data from fire glass suppliers, they are busy with window certification schemes and have sufficient growth across Europe, Poland, Lithuania, Turkey, and with American certification bodies, making fire doors not part of their current plans.

28b877dce3.q: How did joining ER Certification become a turning point in a long fenestration career?
28b877dce3.a: When John joined ER Certification, the potential earnings were lower than he was accustomed to, but he could see the potential. Because of his industry connections and reputation, he was able to bring clients to the business, and that first year more than doubled his expected earnings. The company has continued growing from strength to strength since then.
